turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, Mrs Hale. Sorry, we've run over, the morning list was a bit of a mess.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh don't worry yourself, we were sat in that car park for ages, the machine only takes cards and my husband had coins, so we walked round to the other entrance, my knees didn't love it but we got here.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mm. We got here.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So it's three months on from the stroke. How have things actually been?

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, it's this left hand, doctor, three months on and it's still a bit weak. I can hold a cup of tea now, which I couldn't manage in the hospital, but buttons are a proper nightmare, and if I try to write with the left one it's just scribbles.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the walking? You were unsteady on the ward, as I remember.

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Walking's much better, actually. I go to the shops and back, that's about ten minutes, and I don't need the stick indoors anymore. Outdoors I still take it if the pavement's uneven, and I had one wobble by the post box last week, but I didn't fall, I just grabbed the rail.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's quicker on her feet than she was. Speech-wise I'd say she's back to normal, she doesn't stop talking, as you can tell.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And how does the speech feel to you, Mrs Hale?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh the words are fine now. For the first fortnight I was muddling things, I'd call the kettle the fridge, that sort of nonsense, but that's gone. I do get tired if I talk for a long stretch, like at my sister's last Sunday, but the speaking itself is clear.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or shortness of breath when you do that walk to the shops?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no cough at all, and I'm not breathless on that walk. I puff a tiny bit on the hill by the church but I've always done that, that's the hill, not my chest.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that, not even a twinge.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): And fever. Have you been feeling hot, or shivery?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, not a fever exactly. I feel a bit warm in the evenings, I end up taking my cardigan off, but I haven't been shivery, and I haven't put a thermometer on myself, so I don't really know what you'd call it.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me check the tablets you're actually taking.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Every morning I take the aspirin, seventy-five milligrams, little white tablet, they said it's to stop me having another stroke, and I keep it in a blue box so I don't mix the mornings up. And at night it's the cholesterol one, atorvastin, eighty milligrams, which is a bigger tablet.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every night, the atorvastatin?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, most nights. If I'm shattered I forget it, maybe once or twice in a week, I'm not going to sit here and pretend I don't. I leave it by the kettle so I'll see it, but if we eat late it gets missed.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I do remind her when I'm still up. I'm not always.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): And the blood pressure one is amlodipine, five milligrams, one tablet in the morning. I've had the high blood pressure for years, since well before the stroke, and it's still a thing, obviously, or I wouldn't be on it.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else on top of those three?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister keeps on at me to take biotin, like she does, great big capsules from the chemist for her nails, she reckons my hair's gone thin since March. I've never taken it and I don't intend to, it isn't even prescribed.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And the metformin in the cupboard is mine, for my diabetes. She doesn't take that.

[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fine, your sister's biotin and your husband's metformin stay out of your list. I was going to put the amlodipine up to ten milligrams, because your last pressure was one-forty, and after a stroke I like it lower than that.

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hang on, I'm reading the wrong bit. I thought the top number was one nineteen over eighty, but that's a smudge, the nurse has written one oh nine over seventy-seven, pulse seventy-two, temperature thirty-eight point three.

[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight's fifty-two kilos, and last time in March you were sixty-eight, so that's a fair drop. Forget the increase, we'll leave the amlodipine at five, I don't want you light-headed on a pressure like that.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I know I've got thinner. I don't fancy a proper meal, I pick at bits, it's been the last three months. Cooking with this hand is awkward so my husband does it, he lives with me, but I still leave half of it, which feels rude after he's bothered.
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does leave half. Every evening.

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thirty-eight point three is warmer than I'd like. You say the evenings feel warm but no shivers. It might just be the rush getting here, but I can't completely rule out a mild infection, and I'm not starting antibiotics on that alone.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me see the hand. Squeeze. The grip's a bit weaker on the left, nothing dramatic. No swelling, and the skin looks fine.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the same weakness since I came out, doctor, not a new thing, maybe a fraction better with the cup. I still drop a fork now and then if I'm not looking, and zips are worse than buttons if I'm honest, which is annoying when you're trying to get a coat on.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, err, thinking it through. This is residual weakness from the mild stroke, not a fresh event. The walking and the speech have settled, and the hand hasn't suddenly changed.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to book an MRI of the head to be on the safe side. But no, hearing all that, we'll not do a scan. It wouldn't change what we do today.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I will arrange is bloods, the cholesterol and a liver test, because of the atorvastatin. I nearly said have them before you leave, but the phlebotomy queue is out the door, so I'll book them for this week at your surgery instead.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): This week is fine, I'll put it on the calendar in big letters, otherwise it'll go the way of the night tablet. Do I keep taking the eighty milligrams until those results, or do you want me to stop it?
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep taking it, eighty milligrams every night, don't stop. Set an alarm on your phone if the kettle trick fails. And don't start the biotin, there's no reason to.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep using that left hand for the little jobs, buttons included, even if it's slow. Stick outdoors when the pavement's uneven. And the walk to the shops, keep that up, it's doing you good.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in this clinic in three months. if the hand suddenly gets weaker, or the speech goes off again, don't sit on it, come straight back.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll keep the walks up, I like getting out. I do worry, though, my mum had a stroke when she was seventy-two, and she never really got the use of her arm back, so I overthink every tingle, which is probably not helpful.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your mum's stroke is worth knowing, thank you. What I'm seeing today is steady, not that story. Bloods this week, same tablets, and I'll see you in three months. Mind how you go.

spec.situation: Patient three months after a mild stroke with a spouse; slight weakness in the left hand; takes aspirin, atorvastatin and an amlodipine tablet; blood pressure read aloud; walking and speech discussed.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Walking unsteadiness is improved/currently better, not resolved; wobble was last week, not onset.
bad.text: Walking unsteadiness (category=neurological, status=resolved, onset=last week, temporality=past, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Dose/status supported, but 'every night' is imperfect; patient misses once or twice weekly.
bad.text: atorvastatin (dose=80 mg, frequency=every night, indication=cholesterol, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Walking unsteadiness is recorded wrongly as resolved/onset last week; the patient said walking is much better but not fully resolved, still uses a stick outdoors on uneven pavement and had one wobble last week without a fall.
No fall with the wobble last week; she grabbed the rail and did not fall.
Speech is back to normal/clear now per patient and caregiver.
No fever was not established; the patient said 'not a fever exactly', feels warm in the evenings, has not checked a temperature, and does not know if it counts as fever.
Atorvastatin adherence detail: she misses it maybe once or twice a week if shattered/eating late.
Amlodipine dose increase to 10 mg was considered but then cancelled after reviewing the correct blood pressure reading; plan is to leave it at 5 mg to avoid light-headedness.
Marked weight loss detail: weight was 68 kg in March and is now 52 kg.
Poor intake detail: she does not fancy a proper meal, picks at bits, often leaves half of meals, for the last three months.
Cooking is awkward because of the weak hand.
Additional hand-function symptoms: still drops a fork now and then if not looking; zips are worse than buttons.
The doctor considered booking an MRI head scan but decided not to do a scan because it would not change management today.
Blood tests are to be done this week at her GP surgery because the phlebotomy queue was too long to do them before she left.
